cells.tense: You are here with the work, and it moves through your hands before it moves anywhere else
cells.ask: Write tomorrow's one small act of care and the distinction behind it, two lines, then stop — you'll find out whether you actually picked it or only recognized it, and that finding stays with you
cells.core: You sit at the bench with one plant in front of you and you can tell what it needs this week. Not the whole garden, not the list in your head — the one thing, at this week's size. You can put the rest down without guilt because you know it isn't yours yet, and the plant you kept gets your hands. Nobody has to remind you which is which.\n\nThat sorting is quiet and nobody watches it happen. It's the step people skip, and skipping it is why their care ends up watering the wrong pot. Yours lands where it lands because you don't skip it — you check the soil before you pour, and the deciding underneath does more than the doing on top.
cells.sheetLine: You can tell what deserves the care this week, and you're giving it that.
cells.verb: working the distinctions by hand until the next true thing is unmistakable
cells.place: the bench where something small is put in the ground and left to do the rest

cells.tense: You are living out ahead of the next clear step, in a week that hasn't had a chance to arrive
cells.ask: Pick the one thing you're moving first and say one sentence to the person involved: this step gets your hands first, the rest keeps. Then stop — you'll find out how much of the motion was the future's and how much was yours
cells.core: You fuss over the small thing in front of you and leave the rest alone until it's ready. That's the shape at the bench when your hands are on the right week — one plant, its own pace, nothing forced, and you can wait on it without your shoulders coming up.\n\nRight now the sorting has turned into checking, and checking doesn't finish. You can work at where this is heading harder than anyone asked and still not have it, because the future isn't the project. This week is. The bench is covered in seed packets for a season that hasn't started, and the plant that's actually growing has gone unwatered. The thing that used to feed the growing has started feeding itself.

cells.tense: You are still standing at the place where the care used to happen, waiting until you're sure before it starts again
cells.ask: Ask one specific person for one specific thing and hand them the one thing you'd actually give in return, both small, and let the exchange be plain — you'll see the next thing move, and that answers more than thinking does
cells.core: A small thing gets its next step when you hand over one thing and someone hands you another, no earning first. That's the shape at the bench when the work is moving — simple exchange, both hands busy, the plant getting what it needs from two directions at once.\n\nThe fine sense of what matters is still with you, but it isn't reaching your hands any more. You can see what the plant needs and you wait until you're sure, and the waiting has gotten long. The pots are lined up and nothing has gone in. What turns it back isn't more care. It's the small give-and-take, close enough to happen today.
cells.sheetLine: You can still see what deserves care. It hasn't reached your hands in a while.

cells.tense: You are already steering what gets tended and what gets let go, and you're calling it how the week went
cells.ask: Read back your last two weeks and write one sentence naming the rule that actually governed your time — this came first, for this reason — then say the sentence to one person without asking them anything
cells.core: You pick what gets cared for by attention and by what you let slip, and the picking gets called the schedule. The steering is running either way, at the bench and between the lines of the week — one plant gets moved to the sun and another quietly doesn't.\n\nWhen it works, the rule is visible, mostly to you — one line about why this plant and not that one, sayable out loud without dressing it up. The care is already happening. Saying the rule out loud is the part that hasn't been done, and it's smaller than it sounds.
cells.sheetLine: You're already steering what gets tended. You're calling it the schedule.

attempts.check: I am attributing to the person particular smugness or a particular contradiction between wanting to control outcomes and knowing that you cannot force them; the record does not establish any personal history, motive, or feeling, only the capacity and its seat. The reader might reasonably say: I do not recognize this, I can sit with what I cannot control without distress, and I do the tending on purpose. The ask survives either way, because it is one private written distinction about the next physical thing to be done, and it teaches whether the adjusting is actually happening or happening on purpose. The sentence that serves the writer more than the reader is the line about working hardest in the place where working least matters; it sounds clever and does no work, so it is cut.
